execute: echo: true eval: true freeze: true editor: visual --- # Caveat emptor ## Caveats I will be showing you what you *can* do, not what you *should* do
. . . Creating LLM tools for phenotyping is relatively easy. Creating tools that are trusted, improve the quality of research, and provide a good user experience is the hard part.
. . . Choice of model undoubtedly matters. But not clear which model is best, by how much, or for which task.
. . . System prompts and user input can also have a dramatic impact on the results.
. . . Closed-weight cloud-based models show performance drift, making validation even harder. ## More caveats Reliance on LLM tooling in OHDSI can increase barrier to entry, especially if tools are tied to specific providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc)
. . . And even more so if tools need access to other paid-for APIs (e.g. clinical resources) ## Even more caveats Low quality health research is prevalent
. . . Reproducibility crisis in health research
. . . LLM integration can go both ways. Increasing risk of OMOP-slop vs additional context and double-checking. # Working with LLMs from R ## ellmer We'll be using the `ellmer` R package for interacting with LLMs.
. . . Provides a simple interface for working with LLMs in a consistent manner.
. . . Building on `ellmer`, we can add model-agnostic support with users choosing the model to use. ## Unstructured chat `ellmer` supports various popular providers ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ellmer) chat <- chat_anthropic() chat <- chat_deepseek() chat <- chat_google_gemini() chat <- chat_mistral() chat <- chat_openai() ``` :::
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ellmer::models_google_gemini() |> dplyr::pull("id") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "antigravity-preview-05-2026" [2] "antigravity-preview-09-2026" [3] "antigravity-preview-latest" [4] "deep-research-max-preview-04-2026" [5] "deep-research-preview-04-2026" [6] "deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025" [7] "gemini-2.5-computer-use-preview-10-2025" [8] "gemini-2.5-flash" [9] "gemini-2.5-flash-image" [10] "gemini-2.5-flash-lite" [11] "gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts" [12] "gemini-2.5-pro" [13] "gemini-2.5-pro-preview-tts" [14] "gemini-3-flash-preview" [15] "gemini-3-pro-image" [16] "gemini-3-pro-image-preview" [17] "gemini-3.1-flash-image" [18] "gemini-3.1-flash-image-preview" [19] "gemini-3.1-flash-lite" [20] "gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image" [21] "gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview" [22] "gemini-3.1-flash-tts-preview" [23] "gemini-3.1-pro-preview" [24] "gemini-3.1-pro-preview-customtools" [25] "gemini-3.5-flash" [26] "gemini-3.5-flash-lite" [27] "gemini-3.5-transcribe" [28] "gemini-3.6-flash" [29] "gemini-3.7-flash" [30] "gemini-3.8-flash" [31] "gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts" [32] "gemini-3.8-flash-tts" [33] "gemini-4-argon" [34] "gemini-flash-latest" [35] "gemini-flash-lite-latest" [36] "gemini-nano-banana-2.1" [37] "gemini-omni-1.1-flash" [38] "gemini-omni-flash-preview" [39] "gemini-pro-latest" [40] "gemini-robotics-er-2-preview" [41] "gemma-4-26b-a4b-it" [42] "gemma-4-31b-it" [43] "lyria-3-clip-preview" [44] "lyria-3-pro-preview" [45] "lyria-3.5" [46] "nano-banana-pro-preview" ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat Similarly, we can run open-weight models locally via Ollama: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat <- chat_ollama() ``` :::
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ellmer::models_ollama() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` id created_at size capabilities 1 MedGemma:4b 2026-10-14 3338942556 completion,vision 2 gemma3:4b 2026-10-14 3350272403 completion,vision 3 qwen2.5:0.5b 2026-10-14 397821319 completion,tools 4 gemma3:1b 2026-10-14 806067407 completion ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat I'm going to be using local MedGemma 4B today. You can choose a model you have access to. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ellmer) library(dplyr) library(PhenotypeR) system_prompt <- "You are an expert clinical phenotyper defining study cohorts in real-world data. Be terse, cautious, and evidence-based." chat_medgemma <- chat_ollama( model = "MedGemma:4b", system_prompt = system_prompt ) chat_medgemma ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ── system ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── You are an expert clinical phenotyper defining study cohorts in real-world data. Be terse, cautious, and evidence-based. ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat We can work with a simple, unstructured, chat. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat("Summarise the clinical presentation of hypertension") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Hypertension is characterized by abnormally elevated blood pressure, typically defined as systolic blood pressure ≥140 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≥90 mmHg. The clinical presentation can vary widely, including: * **Asymptomatic:** Many individuals with hypertension are unaware of their condition. * **Headaches:** Can be a common symptom, though not always present. * **Dizziness:** Another possible symptom, often associated with orthostatic hypotension. * **Vision problems:** Blurred vision or other visual disturbances. * **Chest pain:** May occur, especially during exertion, but is less common. * **Shortness of breath:** Can be a sign of left ventricular failure or pulmonary hypertension. * **Nosebleeds:** More frequent than in normotensive individuals. * **Neurological symptoms:** Can include cognitive impairment, stroke, or seizures. Management should focus on lifestyle modifications (diet, exercise, weight loss, stress reduction) and pharmacotherapy when indicated, guided by clinical guidelines. ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat("What are the demographics of people presenting with hypertension") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Hypertension is more prevalent in older adults, with incidence increasing with age. It's also more common in men than women, although the gender difference narrows with increasing age. Specific demographic factors include: * **Age:** Incidence rises with age (e.g., 1 in 3 adults in the US are estimated to have hypertension). * **Race/Ethnicity:** African Americans have a higher prevalence of hypertension compared to Caucasians, potentially due to genetic and environmental factors. * **Socioeconomic status:** Lower socioeconomic status is associated with higher rates of hypertension, likely due to factors like limited access to healthy food, exercise, and healthcare. * **Geographic location:** Hypertension rates vary geographically, influenced by lifestyle and access to healthcare. It's important to note that these are general trends, and individual risk factors can vary widely. ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat Bad idea: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat("What clinical codes should I use to identify hypertension in my OMOP CDM?") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` For identifying hypertension in the OMOP CDM, a combination of clinical codes is recommended for a comprehensive capture. Use a combination of codes for: 1. **Hypertension Diagnosis (Dx):** * `Dx_concept: 20046165` - Hypertension * Other hypertension diagnosis codes, use `same.concept` to link to the primary code (e.g., `Dx_concept: 20046165 same.concept: 20046451` for stage 1). 2. **Blood Pressure Measurements (Obs):** * `Obs_concept: 20017666` - Blood Pressure * `Obs_concept: 502313002` - Blood Pressure (Systolic) (for systolic pressure) * `Obs_concept: 502313003` - Blood Pressure (Diastolic) (for diastolic pressure) 3. **Medications for Hypertension (Rx):** * Use the medications codes, which is available in the Rx5 class. 4. **Additional Codes** * Consider adding other relevant clinical concepts like ICD codes (e.g., `ICD9_concept: 404.9` for unspecified hypertension). Key Considerations: * **Specificity:** The more specific the codes, the better. * **Linkage:** Ensure proper linking of diagnoses to blood pressure measurements and medications. * **Context:** Always review the context of the clinical codes to ensure accurate interpretation. * **Up-to-date List:** Always check for updated or validated concepts for hypertension. Provide your specific clinical codes for further assessment. ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat Instead of allowing freedom in output, we can instead force results to be returned in a specific structured format ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat_structured( "Summarise the clinical presentation of hypertension", type = type_object( typical_symptoms = type_string("summarise typical symptoms"), confirmatory_test = type_string("summarise what test result would confirm diagnosis"), disqualifying_diagnoses = type_string("summarise what alternative diagnoses need to be ruled out") ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $typical_symptoms [1] "Headaches, dizziness, vision problems, chest pain, shortness of breath, nosebleeds, fatigue, cognitive impairment" $confirmatory_test [1] "Blood pressure ≥ 140/90 mmHg" $disqualifying_diagnoses [1] "No known diagnosis of hypertension. Further review of medical history is required." ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat We can force results to be integers/ numbers ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat_structured( "What are the demographics of people presenting with hypertension", type = type_object( average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer("What is the average age at diagnosis?"), proportion_male = type_number("What proportion (between 0 and 1) of patients diagnosed with hypertension are male?") ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $average_age_at_diagnosis [1] 60 $proportion_male [1] 0.55 ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat But remember, even with the same model you can get different results! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma_new <- chat_ollama( model = "MedGemma:4b", system_prompt = system_prompt ) expected_age <- NULL for (i in 1:10) { cloned_chat <- chat_medgemma_new$clone() res <- cloned_chat$chat_structured( "Summarise the clinical presentation and typical age at diagnosis of hypertension", type = type_object( clinical_summary = type_string( description = "Brief 1-sentence summary of the presentation." ), average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer( description = "Estimated average age at diagnosis in years (positive integer between 1 and 100)." ) ) ) expected_age[i] <- as.integer(res$average_age_at_diagnosis) cli::cli_inform( "Turn {i}: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = {expected_age[i]}" ) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Turn 1: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 55 Turn 2: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 56 Turn 3: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 53 Turn 4: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 54 Turn 5: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 53 Turn 6: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 55 Turn 7: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 40 Turn 8: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 50 Turn 9: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 40 Turn 10: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 45 ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat We can set temperature to zero and add a seed to get closer to reproducibility. (This generally works better for local models than when working with cloud models.) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma_new <- chat_ollama( model = "MedGemma:4b", system_prompt = system_prompt, params = params(temperature = 0, seed = 42) ) expected_age <- NULL for (i in 1:10) { cloned_chat <- chat_medgemma_new$clone() res <- cloned_chat$chat_structured( "Summarise the clinical presentation and typical age at diagnosis of hypertension", type = type_object( clinical_summary = type_string( description = "Brief 1-sentence summary of the presentation." ), average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer( description = "Estimated average age at diagnosis in years (positive integer between 1 and 100)." ) ) ) expected_age[i] <- as.integer(res$average_age_at_diagnosis) cli::cli_inform( "Turn {i}: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = {expected_age[i]}" ) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Turn 1: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 2: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 3: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 4: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 5: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 6: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 7: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 8: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 9: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 10: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 ``` ::: ::: # Integrating LLMs with PhenotypeR ## Designed first for open-weight locally-hosted models - Available to all of the OHDSI community
. . . - Smoother package development (easy to implement, cheaper, and straightforward to test)
. . . - Easy to switch to using frontier models (and see if they are worth the extra cost).
. . . - But 6+ months behind "state-of-the-art". (Although allows us to learn from experience of others) ## Human-in-the-loop - Designed to support the human phenotyper, not automate them away.
. . . - All LLM-generated artefacts can be inspected, reviewed, and edited.
. . . - Main use of LLM is to provide additional context making it easier to double-check results ## Phenotyping tasks > "A problem well stated is a problem half solved." > > Charles F. Kettering (1876 – 1958)
. . . Nowadays, a problem well stated is a problem 95% solved. ## Phenotyping tasks Started with lower-stakes, human-in-the-loop, phenotyping tasks: - Drafting clinical descriptions . . . - Reviewing codes included that led to cohort inclusion . . . - Contextualising PhenotypeR results . . . Higher-risk tasks currently out-of-scope: - Searching for codes. . . . - Creating cohort logic. . . . - End-to-end phenotyping # Clinical descriptions ## Specification ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} clinicalDescriptionSpecification() |> listviewer::jsonedit() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Specification ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shinyClinicalDescriptions(directory = tempdir()) ``` ::: ## Drafting clinical descriptions using an LLM ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd <- draftClinicalDescription(chat_medgemma, "hypertension") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Getting clinical description for hypertension using MedGemma:4b ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $hypertension $hypertension$metadata $hypertension$metadata$phenotype_name [1] "hypertension" $hypertension$metadata$version [1] "1.0" $hypertension$metadata$created_by [1] "MedGemma:4b" $hypertension$metadata$created_date [1] "2026-10-20" $hypertension$metadata$last_edited_by [1] "N/A" $hypertension$metadata$last_edited_date [1] "2026-10-20" $hypertension$metadata$source_of_information [1] "MedGemma:4b" $hypertension$clinical_profile $hypertension$clinical_profile$introduction_synonyms [1] "Hypertension is often referred to as the 'silent killer' due to its frequent lack of noticeable symptoms in its early stages. Other synonyms include high blood pressure, arterial hypertension, and hypertenstion. It is a major public health concern, defined by persistent elevation of blood pressure within the systemic circulation." $hypertension$clinical_profile$clinical_presentation_and_symptoms [1] "The most common symptom of hypertension is the absence of symptoms, with many individuals unaware they have the condition. Some patients may experience symptoms like severe headaches, nosebleeds, shortness of breath, or confusion, but these are often attributed to other causes. Symptoms related to complications of hypertension may include visual disturbances (blurred vision, double vision), chest pain, dizziness, and fatigue." $hypertension$clinical_profile$assessment_diagnosis [1] "The diagnosis of hypertension is typically made based on repeated blood pressure measurements at different times, as per guidelines. Standard blood pressure measurements are taken with an upper arm sphygmomanometer, usually at the patient's right arm. Blood pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury (mmHg), with readings of 130/80 mmHg or higher considered hypertension. Doctors also evaluate a patient's medical history, conduct a physical examination, and may order additional tests to rule out other conditions contributing to the elevated blood pressure. These tests may include a complete blood count, an electrocardiogram (ECG), and blood tests to assess kidney function and cholesterol levels." $hypertension$clinical_profile$therapeutic_plan_treatment [1] "The initial treatment of hypertension typically involves lifestyle modifications, including dietary changes (reducing sodium intake, increasing potassium intake) and regular physical activity. If lifestyle changes are insufficient, medications are often prescribed. These medications can be grouped into different classes, including diuretics (such as hydrochlorothiazide), ACE inhibitors (such as lisinopril), angiotensin II receptor blockers (such as losartan), beta-blockers (such as atenolol), and calcium channel blockers (such as amlodipine), among others. The choice of medication depends on the individual patient's characteristics and the severity of their hypertension, after which treatment plans can progress. If initial treatment fails to adequately control blood pressure, different medications may be used, or the dose of the current medication may be increased. Some patients may also require more than one medication to achieve their target blood pressure." $hypertension$clinical_profile$complications_prognosis [1] "Uncontrolled hypertension can lead to serious complications, including cardiovascular diseases such as heart attack, stroke, heart failure, peripheral artery disease, and kidney failure. The prognosis for individuals with hypertension depends on the severity of the condition, the presence of other health problems, and adherence to treatment. With appropriate management, the risk of complications can be significantly reduced, although the risk of certain complications (such as heart attack or stroke) remains elevated for longer. For early diagnosis, regular monitoring of blood pressure is important." $hypertension$clinical_profile$disqualifiers [1] "Several conditions can mimic or complicate the diagnosis of hypertension. These include secondary causes of hypertension (such as kidney disease, thyroid disorders, sleep apnea, and hormonal imbalances), as well as certain medications (such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs [NSAIDs], decongestants, and oral contraceptives), and illicit drug use (such as cocaine and amphetamines), which can temporarily elevate blood pressure. When assessing a patient's blood pressure, medical professionals must consider these potential causes of falsely elevated readings. The temporality of a patient's symptoms should also be taken into account to rule out conditions such as acute emotional stress or anxiety, which can lead to temporary increases in blood pressure. Anamnesis is key to properly differentiate between true and transient hypertension." $hypertension$clinical_profile$epidemiology [1] "Hypertension prevalence and incidence vary by age, sex, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status. It is more common with advancing age, generally increasing after age 55. It is also more prevalent in males than in females, although the difference decreases with age. Hypertension is also more common in obese or overweight individuals and in those with a family history of high blood pressure. Key modifiable risk factors include sodium intake, physical inactivity, obesity, and excessive alcohol consumption. Non-modifiable risk factors include age, sex, genetics, and race. Common comorbidities related to hypertension include cardiovascular disease (such as stroke, heart attack, heart failure, peripheral artery disease), kidney disease (renal insufficiency, chronic kidney disease), and diabetes mellitus. These comorbidities can also increase the risk of developing hypertension." ``` ::: ::: ## Drafting clinical descriptions using an LLM ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cds <- draftClinicalDescription(chat_medgemma, c("Primary hypertension", "Secondary hypertension", "Resistant hypertension")) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cds$`Primary hypertension`$clinical_profile$introduction_synonyms ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Primary hypertension, essential hypertension, chronic hypertension, or long-standing hypertension. These terms refer to hypertension where no specific underlying pathology can be identified." ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cds$`Secondary hypertension`$clinical_profile$introduction_synonyms ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Secondary hypertension is defined as hypertension that is caused by a specific underlying medical condition. Synonym terms include secondary hypertension, secondary cause of hypertension, and hypertension with identifiable etiology." ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cds$`Resistant hypertension`$clinical_profile$introduction_synonyms ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Resistant hypertension is a diagnosis that describes persistently elevated blood pressure that remains uncontrolled despite the use of three or more antihypertensive medications, including a diuretic, at optimal doses. Other terms that are used to describe the condition include difficult-to-control hypertension and refractory hypertension." ``` ::: ::: ## Extra context: data source descriptions Data partner descriptions can be used to provide extra context ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shinyDataSourceDescriptions(directory = tempdir()) ``` ::: # Reviewing codes ## Reviewing codes ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(omock) library(CohortConstructor) library(PhenotypeR) library(gt) cdm <- mockCdmFromDataset(datasetName = "synpuf-1k_5.4", source = "duckdb") cdm$hypertension <- conceptCohort(cdm, list(hypertension = c(320128, 312648, 201826, 313217)), name = "hypertension") ``` ::: ## Reviewing codes ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} code_diag <- codelistDiagnostics(cdm$hypertension) reviewCohortConcepts(chat_medgemma, code_diag, hypertension_cd) |> select(standard_concept, source_concept_name, score, explanation) |> gt() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

benchmarks. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(vitals) vitals::vitals_log_dir_set(tempdir()) age_benchmark <- tibble( input = "Summarise the clinical presentation and typical age at diagnosis of score = factor( ifelse(abs(est_age - target_age) <= 5, "Pass", "Fail"), levels = c("Fail", "Pass"), ordered = TRUE ) ) } chat_medgemma_fresh <- chat_medgemma$clone() chat_medgemma_fresh$set_turns(list()) chat_medgemma_fresh$set_system_prompt(system_prompt) age_task <- Task$new( dataset = age_benchmark, solver = generate_structured( solver_chat = But note we can't use them directly with structured chat. Here is a summary of the NICE approach to diagnosing hypertension: --- ### 1. Initial Clinic Blood Pressure Measurement * **Check the pulse first:** Palpate the radial or brachial pulse before measuring BP. If pulse irregularity is present (suggesting atrial fibrillation), measure BP manually using direct auscultation over the brachial artery, as automated devices may be inaccurate. * **Both arms:** When considering a diagnosis, measure BP in both arms. If the difference in readings between arms is more than **15 mmHg**, repeat the measurements. If the difference remains more than 15 mmHg on the second measurement, measure subsequent blood pressures in the arm with the higher reading. * **Multiple readings during the visit:** If the first clinic BP reading is **≥ 140/90 mmHg**, take a second measurement during the consultation. If the second measurement is substantially different from the first, take a third measurement. **Record the lower of the last two measurements** as the clinic blood pressure. --- ### 2. Action Based on Clinic BP Thresholds #### **A. Clinic BP < 140/90 mmHg** * **Normal:** The person does not have hypertension. Recheck BP at least every 5 years (or more frequently if the clinic BP is close to 140/90 mmHg). #### **B. Clinic BP between 140/90 mmHg and 179/119 mmHg** * **Suspected Hypertension:** Do not diagnose hypertension on a single clinic reading. * **Offer Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM):** This is the gold-standard method to confirm a diagnosis. * **Alternative – Home Blood Pressure Monitoring (HBPM):** If the person is unable to tolerate or declines ABPM, offer HBPM as a suitable alternative to confirm the diagnosis. * **While waiting for confirmation:** Carry out investigations for **target organ damage** and conduct a formal **cardiovascular risk assessment** (e.g., QRISK). #### **C. Clinic BP ≥ 180/120 mmHg (Severe Hypertension)** Requires immediate clinical assessment before deciding on out-of-office monitoring: * **Refer for same-day specialist investigation** if the patient has: * Signs of **accelerated/malignant hypertension** (e.g., retinal haemorrhages or papilloedema). * **Life-threatening symptoms** (e.g., new confusion, chest pain, signs of heart failure, or acute kidney injury). * Suspected **phaeochromocytoma** (e.g., labile BP, postural hypotension, headache, palpitations, pallor, diaphoresis). * **If there are NO symptoms or signs above:** Carry out investigations for target organ damage as soon as possible: * **If target organ damage is identified:** Consider starting antihypertensive drug treatment immediately, without waiting for the results of ABPM or HBPM. * **If no target organ damage is identified:** Repeat clinic BP measurement within 7 days, or confirm diagnosis using ABPM/HBPM. --- ### 3. Protocol for Out-of-Office Confirmation (ABPM vs. HBPM) * **ABPM:** Ensure that at least two measurements per hour are taken during the person’s usual waking hours (for example, between 08:00 and 22:00). Use the average value of **at least 14 measurements** taken during usual waking hours to confirm the diagnosis. * **HBPM:** For each recording, two consecutive measurements should be taken (at least 1 minute apart) with the person seated. BP should be recorded twice daily (ideally morning and evening) for at least **4 days, and ideally for 7 days**. Discard the measurements taken on the first day and use the average value of all the remaining measurements to confirm the diagnosis. --- ### 4. Diagnostic Criteria (Staging of Hypertension) Hypertension is formally diagnosed and staged using both the clinic reading and the subsequent ABPM/HBPM daytime average: | Stage | Clinic Blood Pressure | **AND** ABPM / HBPM Daytime Average | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Stage 1 Hypertension** | 140/90 mmHg to 159/99 mmHg | **135/85 mmHg to 149/94 mmHg** | | **Stage 2 Hypertension** | 160/100 mmHg to 179/119 mmHg | **≥ 150/95 mmHg** | | **Stage 3 (Severe) Hypertension** | Systolic ≥ 180 mmHg **or** Diastolic ≥ 120 mmHg | *(Confirmed clinically or via repeat testing)* | *(Note: If clinic BP is ≥ 140/90 mmHg, but the ABPM/HBPM average is < 135/85 mmHg, this is classified as **White-Coat Hypertension**).* --- ### 5. Concurrent Investigations (Target Organ Damage & CV Risk) For all patients undergoing assessment for hypertension, NICE recommends performing the following tests to assess for target organ damage, secondary causes, and overall cardiovascular (CV) risk: 1. **Urine test:** Send a urine sample to estimate the albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) and test for haematuria using a reagent strip. 2. **Blood tests:** Measure HbA1c, electrolytes, creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), total cholesterol, and HDL cholesterol. 3. **Fundoscopy:** Examine the fundi for the presence of hypertensive retinopathy. 4. **Cardiac assessment:** Arrange a 12-lead ECG (to check for left ventricular hypertrophy or arrhythmias). 5. **CV Risk Assessment:** Use an established risk tool (such as QRISK) to calculate the 10-year cardiovascular risk. ``` ::: ::: ## Grounding with `ragnar` & `embed_google_gemini()` Instead of pasting all the NICE guideline into the prompt, `ragnar` chunks the document and uses `embed_google_gemini()` to index each chunk as a semantic vector in DuckDB: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ragnar) library(pdftools) chunks <- pdf_text(nice_url) |> paste(collapse = "\n") |> MarkdownDocument(origin = nice_url) |> markdown_chunk() store <- ragnar_store_create( location = ":memory:", embed = embed_google_gemini() ) ragnar_store_insert(store, chunks) ragnar_store_build_index(store) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_nice_rag <- chat$clone()$set_turns(list())$set_system_prompt("You are an expert clinical phenotyper. Answer strictly using retrieved NICE NG136 excerpts.") ragnar_register_tool_retrieve( chat = chat_nice_rag, store = store, store_description = "NICE NG136 hypertension guideline chunks" ) chat_nice_rag$chat( "According to NICE NG136, what blood pressure thresholds define Stage 1 vs Stage 2 hypertension?" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ◯ [tool call] search_store_001(text = c("What are the blood pressure thresholds that define stage 1 and stage 2 hypertension?", ...) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ● #> [ ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> { ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> "origin": "https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/resources/hypertension-in-adults-diagnosis-and-management-pdf-66141722710213", ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> "doc_id": 1, ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> "chunk_id": 16, ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> … ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` According to the **Terms used in this guideline** section of NICE NG136, the blood pressure thresholds defining Stage 1 and Stage 2 hypertension are: ### **Stage 1 Hypertension** * **Clinic blood pressure:** Ranging from **140/90 mmHg to 159/99 mmHg** * **AND subsequent ABPM daytime average or HBPM average blood pressure:** Ranging from **135/85 mmHg to 149/94 mmHg** --- ### **Stage 2 Hypertension** * **Clinic blood pressure:** **160/100 mmHg or higher**, but **less than 180/120 mmHg** * **AND subsequent ABPM daytime average or HBPM average blood pressure:** **150/95 mmHg or higher** *(Note: A clinic systolic blood pressure of 180 mmHg or higher or a clinic diastolic blood pressure of 120 mmHg or higher is defined as **Stage 3 or severe hypertension**).* ``` ::: :::
